Hi Auriel, how many sites do you have?  There are other examples/discussions here of folks "stacking" replicates of sites into new sites for various unmarked models.  There are potential issues with the approach (psuedoreplication) but it can sometimes also be reasonable.  It's important to understand how your inferences are affected.

What kind of covariates are associated with the primary periods?  If they are common to all sites and vary only across periods, you are pretty limited with what you can specify and would not be able to include primary period as a factor in addition to a period-specific covariate.  But if they vary across both sites and primary periods, you have more flexibility.

messages.body_plain:
Don, the Sillet et al. 2012 paper does have distance data, but they do not actually estimate phi using multiple replicates.  They used the gdistsamp function to take advantage of the negative binomial distribution for abundance.  This is pointed out in the help file (?gdistsamp) where Richard notes that setting numPrimary=1 will give you the same results as distsamp but allow examination of the NB distribution.  Sillet et al. 2012 used 3 distance bands as indicated in their code:

db <- c(0, 100, 200, 300)

If you have R sites, J distance bands, and T occasions, you need a matrix y that is R x JT with the count of individuals for each band at each occasion. The data files in Sillet et al. 2012 are R=307, J=3, and T=1 (fall and spring data, separate).  As another example, with J=3 and T=2, your column names could look like this:

colnames(y) <- c("band1visit1", "band2visit1","band3visit1","band1visit2", "band2visit2","band3visit2")

The unmarkedFrameGDS object doesn't need column names for y but it might help with your data organization.  Experienced R users simplify their code to increase readability and efficiency so sometimes things aren't obvious.  But it is best to dig into the help files and work with examples, like Richard has provided, to better understand.  The help file for gdistsamp does have everything you need, but you have to spend time with it.

In this case, can I make inferences based on the model selection procedure using colext  and then make occupancy predictions for each season separately using occuPEN? This seems appropriate, somehow?

Thank you very much

Best regards

Marconi Campos

Extra first line for years, I suppose.
Empty cells.

yearlySiteCovs = data.frame(year = year, agua = as.numeric(unlist(t(a[,33:38]))))

obsCovs <-data.frame(secondary = as.factor(rep(c(1,2,3,4,5),S*T)))

umf = unmarkedMultFrame(y = y, siteCovs = site.cov, yearlySiteCovs = yearlySiteCovs, obsCovs = obsCovs, numPrimary = 6)

On Monday, October 5, 2015 at 12:01:52 PM UTC-5, Kery Marc wrote:
> Dear all,
>
> we have now mentioned our new book a couple of times on this list, so let's make it official and formal once and for all.
>
> Our new book Applied hierarchical modeling in ecology (Academic Press, 2016), or AHM for short, provides an up-to-date synthesis on the hierarchical modeling of abundance, occurrence and community metrics such as species richness in what we call "meta-population designs". By the latter, we mean the very common case where you have measured these things at multiple sites. That is, the typical data collection protocol for occupancy and N-mixture models etc. Not surprisingly, one big feature of almost all the models in our book is an explicit model component for measurement error (that is, typically for false-negative errors).
>
> The book is written in a similar style as the legendary "gentle intro to MARK" by Evan Cooch as well as my two earlier books on BUGS for ecologists (Kery, 2010; and Kery & Schaub, 2012). That also means that there are abundant and fully documented code examples, that take you right from the start (e.g., reading data in and formatting them) of an analysis to fitting the model, doing GoF assessments and presenting results, often with the forming of predictions (very important !). We are convinced that ecologists learn statistical modeling best by studying a fully running recipe for an analysis, which they can then take as a template for their own analysis.
>
> We expect this book to be useful for people on this list as well as those on the HMecology list. We fit all models with maximum likelihood (that is, with unmarked) if we can fit them in this way and of course in one of the BUGS engines (in our case, good old WinBUGS and JAGS). For every model type we give an easy intro to the model. As another key feature of our book, we use data simulation to explain a model: showing how you simulate a data set under a model is a very accessible way of describing that model. But of course we also explain each model in equations and in words, and there are some likelihoods around, too.
>
> The book comes in two hefty volumes and we almost feel the need to apologize for that. AHM was originally planned as a single volume, but then we recognized the wealth of material at our hands and our baby grew and so now there will be two volumes. messages.body_plain:
Don,

You can't have missing covariate values for any observations, even ones that did not occur.  And this isn't unique to unmarked, this is a basic linear modeling requirement.  In your case, unmarked is throwing out a site or row any time it has an NA under an observation-level covariate.  Since some (or many) of your sites have at least 1 NA for a given observation, the entire site gets dropped.

One solution is to impute values for the missing covariates that correspond to the mean for actual observations.  There is discussion of this elsewhere on the Google group, and on the internet in general (e.g., StackOverflow), because it is not a perfect solution for a number of reasons.

obs.covs$time[is.na(obs.covs$time)] <- 0   #given standardized covariates

But I think it can generally work well here since the missing covariates are affecting the observation/detection process and not the state process.  For instance, if you had missing site-level covariates, that might be more problematic.  I'm curious what others think about that though.

messages.subject: modelled occurrence as a covariate
messages.body_plain:
Hi Group,

I am estimating occupancy and abundance (using RN model) for several wild ungulate species in Lao PDR. During the survey we also collected data on threats (presence of domestic livestock, presence of snares, and presence of humans) which are predicted to be major determinants of ungulate occurrence/abundance.

Threats are also detected imperfectly so conceptually what I need is two-species co-occurrence model (which makes sense when thinking wild deer and domestic cattle, maybe less so when thinking about wild deer and snares, or humans!). Such models (i.e. Mackenzie et al. 2004) aren’t implemented in unmarked and though at a later date I will look at this in BUGS, I need something quick in the meantime.

Could I just estimate psi for each of the threats, use those values as a covariates in my species models, and then use AIC as normal to test for evidence that they are important predictors of occurrence/abundance? Or is that statistically non-allowable “double-dipping”?

I have some memory of a similar discussion in this forum but I wasn’t able to find it. Apologies if this topic has been dealt with before.

Hannah

messages.subject: Cohorts in MacKenzie-Bailey GOF test for single season occupancy models
messages.subject_clean: Cohorts in MacKenzie-Bailey GOF test for single season occupancy models
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,
MacKenzie and Bailey 2004 recommend a GOF test for the single-species occupancy model based on a Pearson chi-square statistic calculated from the observed and expected counts of given detection histories.  This is implemented in R for unmarked::occu fits as AICcmodavg::mb.chisq

When different sites are visited on different numbers of occasions (so that some detection histories have NAs), MacKenzie and Bailey recommend that sites with different numbers of NAs must be treated as different cohorts.  For example, the expected and observed numbers of histories of the form c(X, X, X, NA) need to be treated separately from histories of the form c(X, X, X, X).  This makes perfect sense.

MacKenzie and Bailey also recommend that histories with the same number of NAs, but with NAs in different positions, be treated as separate cohorts.  My question is why?  [One reason it could matter is if the rank-order of a visit was included as a categorical detection covariate in the model.  But let's assume this isn't the case--that would be a weird thing to do anyway.]  Why should goodness-of-fit statistics be influenced by whether I code my visits as the first, second and third (with a missing fourth), as opposed to first, second, and fourth (with a missing third)?

If I am doing avian point counts at 50 sites for a summer, I could code an NA for every single point that I don't visit on a given day, and end up with 50 cohorts of one site each.  In this absurd case, it obviously would make much more sense to remove all of the NAs except the trailing ones at sites visited fewer than the maximum number of times.

It seems like this should be acceptable practice in general: create a separate cohort for each total number of visits, and remove all the NAs (ignoring which position in the visit sequence they occupy).

One last way of stating my confusion. Consider two study protocols for occupancy surveys:
1) Survey the sites in some order.  If it is raining on the day that is scheduled for the first visit to site J, skip it and code it as NA.
2) Survey the sites in some order.  If it is raining on the day that is scheduled for site J, skip it.  Code the next visit to site J (the first time J is actually sampled) as the first sample from the site.

It is hard for me to imagine that these separate options, that result in the exact same model getting fit to the exact same data, should result in different GOF statistics.  Why not just treat all histories with N visits as a single cohort, regardless of the positions of their NAs?

Best,
Jacob Socolar

I suspect this won;'t come across well, but...better to have it right, than fast. Expediency is an operational consideration, but since the premise is we're doing 'science', then inconveniences on doing it right trump the 'gains' in getting 'a result' quickly. Personally, I;'d rather have the r9ight result, than the 'fast result'. In a perfect worlkd, they're the same.

>
> I don't want to put words in Evan's mouth here but one thing people often recommend in place of what I said (testing the best model) is to test the full model (or the saturated model) and then think about model selection if you have a model that fits.   I don't think that is very practical with the Dail-Madsen model because the models are difficult to fit.  But I'm not sure what Evan would recommend... Evan?

This is, of course, a huge issue at the moment. Our capacity to 'construct' a model, and 'derive estimates' from it has in many instance exceeded our capqability to assess fit of the model to the data in the first place. Sometimes, the problem is conceptual -- a saturated model isn't always defined. In such cases, unclear how to proceed. In other cases, there are numerically intensive resampling approaches which may be the best you can do (the median c-hat,in MARK, derived from some early suggestions by eorge Sevber, is an example of same). The problems with GOF testing are many -- is the lack of fit due to structural incomaptability of the model with the 'true' structure of the data, or is it because of poorly beaving 'animals' who don't understand that they should all flip completely independent multinomial coins for various life events. In my experience, there is a subtle but important conflict between the two -- in the latter case, most folks seem content with estimate some sort of measure of lack of fit (the ubiquitous c-hat), used in some sort of quasi-likelihood adjustment to model selection (via AIC or otherwise). The estimation of c-hat becomes an estimation problem. But, the estimation is not informative -- it doesn't give any clues as to 'why' there is a lack of fit, merely, it estimates the magnitude of the lack of fit. Without knowing why there might be lack of fit, its hard to know if the model structure, given the data, is flawed from the outset. In other words, there is information in lack of fit that might be important (i.e., it isn't like all due to extra-binomial noise).

So, what to do? In the absence of a reasonable abiulity to estimate/parse lack of fit (note: because it might take a long time on a computer does *not* constitute reasonable -- compute time is cheap, realtive to the cost of collecting the data. If it takes hours -> days to run a model, so what, other than the risk that your system crashes before its done), what I've often suggested, which is admitedly ad hoc, but which at least has some conceptual basis, is to evaluate the 'sensitivity' of the model selection criterion (say, randkings based on AIC) to different values of c-hat. Default is 1. Then, you try 1.1, 1.2...2.0 or so. If the basic rank order of models stays more or less constant, you're probably fine/safe. If, on the other hand, you get 'big' jumps in rank order, especially for c-hat in the 1.0 -> 2.0 range, then I'd be pretty suspicious. I did a fairly large simulation experiement at one point that showed that big jumps in rankings often strongly indicated basic structural causes for lack of fit.

As a (somewhat) related aside -- as c-hat goes up, various 'rules of thumb' for using relative normalized AIC weights as the basis for model selection require more thought (since everything gets 'more conservative'). This is treated in some detail in Edwards 'likelihood' book, and in precis form in the MARK book in a couple of places.

At any rate...
